title: Jarasandha Hurls His Mace toward Mathura
story:
From the heights of Girivraja, the mountain-girt capital of Magadha, its king lifted a mace and began to whirl it — once, and again, and ninety-nine turns in all — until the iron seemed less a weapon than the shape of his anger. Then, with everything he had behind it, he hurled it toward Mathura.

The king was Jarasandha, and his quarrel with Krishna was old. Years before, Krishna had slain Kamsa, the cruel king of Mathura, who had married Jarasandha's daughters — and the king of Magadha had never forgiven it. Men who knew them both said it was not a grudge to be taken lightly.

Jarasandha was the son of Vrihadratha, and the story of his rise was told wherever kings gathered. When the great ascetic Chandakausika came into the land of the Magadhas, King Vrihadratha went out to receive him with his ministers, his priest, his wives, and his young son, and in his joy he offered the sage his whole kingdom, and the boy along with it. The sage was pleased. Instead of taking the gift, he gave a prophecy: the boy would grow in prosperity and might beyond every other king; weapons hurled at him, even by the gods themselves, would cause him no pain; he would outshine all who wore crowns, as the sun dims every lesser light; and the kings of the earth would live under his command.

Vrihadratha set the boy on the throne, and, having lost all taste for the world, retired into the woods with his two wives. The prophecy kept its word. Jarasandha ruled his own people like a father, and by his valour he brought king after king under his sway.

And it was this man's mace that now flew toward Mathura, the city where Krishna lived. The weapon fell just outside the city — ninety-nine yojanas from the heights where it had been thrown, a yojana being a measure of many miles — and the place where it struck, lying close to Mathura, came to be called Gadavasan. The citizens saw the whole matter clearly and went to Krishna with the news of its fall.

The name of Jarasandha explained the weight of it. He had two champions, Hansa and Dimvaka, whom no weapon could slay and whose counsel in statecraft and right was counted the finest among men; the two of them together with Jarasandha were held a match, men said, for the three worlds and all that lived in them. It was for that reason that the warrior clans of Krishna's own people — the Vrishnis, the Andhakas, the Kukkurras — had never judged it wise to fight him. And now his strength lay in the earth near Mathura: a throw that had crossed the whole distance between the two cities was also a warning that the army behind the throw could cross it.

Krishna heard the citizens out. The mace lay at Gadavasan, close to the city's edge, and the warning was complete in itself: a weapon that could cover such a distance could be followed by the army that owned it. The citizens had brought their news; what it meant now rested with Krishna.
reflection: A mace hurled across the country was a king's way of drawing a line: the distance from Girivraja to Mathura, measured by his own strength, as a notice that the enmity over Kamsa's death would not quietly fade. The weapon itself was a warning, and it was also an announcement of the long conflict to come.
next_story_tease: But the king of Magadha was only beginning; the time would come when Krishna proposed meeting that strength directly.
hero_scene: Jarasandha, on the high ground of Girivraja, whirling a great mace above his head ninety-nine times with fury, the weapon a dark blur against the sky, aimed far across the plains toward distant Mathura.
